passages.title: Email Correspondence: An Accessible Seat That Was Not

emails.subject: Booking 55-2207, 14 February — wheelchair space
emails.body:
Dear Access Team,

I booked two tickets for the 14 February performance, one wheelchair space and one companion seat. The booking page described the space as "step-free access, level with the stalls".

The space is level with the stalls. It is reached by a corridor with a 40 mm lip at the fire door, which I could not cross unassisted. Two members of your staff lifted the front of my chair over it. They were willing and kind and I want that recorded, because none of what follows is about them.

Being lifted is not step-free access. It is assisted access, which is a different thing that I did not book and would not have booked. I would have chosen a different performance or a different theatre, and the point of an access booking page is to let me make that choice in advance rather than discover it at the door in front of a queue.

I am not asking for a refund; I saw the play and enjoyed it. I am asking that the description be corrected, and I would like to know whether anyone has measured that threshold or whether "step-free" was applied to the route because the route has no steps in it.

Sincerely,
Ravinder Chaudhry

emails.subject: RE: Booking 55-2207, 14 February — wheelchair space
emails.body:
Dear Mr Chaudhry,

Nobody has measured it. Your second explanation is the correct one: "step-free" was applied because the route contains no steps, and a threshold was not treated as a step by whoever wrote the page. That is a definition we adopted without examining, and your email is the first time anyone here has been asked to defend it.

I had the threshold measured on Tuesday. It is 42 mm. The guidance we work to treats anything above 15 mm as a barrier requiring a ramp or a chamfer, so the description was wrong by our own standard and not only by yours.

The booking page now reads "level access with one 42 mm threshold; a portable ramp is available on request at no charge and takes about two minutes to fit". That is accurate, it lets you decide in advance, and it is what should have been there.

The permanent fix is a chamfered threshold plate. It is ordered and the fire officer has approved the specification; installation is scheduled for 11 March. If that slips I will write and tell you rather than let the date pass quietly.

One thing I want to be straight about. We have four other routes described as step-free on that page. I do not know whether they are, because they were described by the same person applying the same definition. All four are being measured this week and I would rather tell you that now than have you find it out later.

Regards,
Colette Nwankwo
Access Manager

passages.title: Marlowe Theatre — Accessible Performances, Spring Season
passages.intro: Season runs March 6 to June 14. Performances marked (C) are captioned; (A) audio-described with a free touch tour 60 minutes before curtain; (R) relaxed, with reduced lighting and sound and freedom to move around. Wheelchair spaces are available at all performances and must be booked by phone. Companion tickets are free with any access booking. Assistance dogs are welcome throughout.

passages.title: What Accessibility Standards Do Not Measure
passages.content:
Accessibility regulation has produced measurable change, and the parts that are easiest to specify are the parts that improved most. That correlation is worth examining, because it explains both the successes and a set of persistent failures that look puzzling otherwise.

Standards are written around features that can be inspected: a ramp gradient, a door width, a lift, a designated space. These are genuine improvements and they are also the elements that can be signed off at completion and never revisited. What is not inspected is whether the feature works as a route. A building can satisfy every individual requirement while the accessible entrance is at the rear, the accessible toilet is used for storage, and the lift requires a key held at a desk on another floor. Each component passes; the journey fails.

The reliability problem is under-recognised and arguably larger than the provision problem. A ramp that exists is not the same as a ramp that is clear of deliveries, and a lift that is installed is not the same as a lift that is working. Surveys of disabled travellers consistently find that unpredictability — not absence — is the dominant complaint, because a journey that might work cannot be planned around. Redundancy matters more than specification: two adequate routes are worth more than one excellent one.

Information is the least regulated element and frequently the decisive one. Where access details are absent, vague or wrong, the effect is the same as inaccessibility, because the person cannot commit to attending. Describing a route as step-free when it contains a threshold is not a small inaccuracy; it converts a decision made in advance into a discovery made on arrival, which is the specific harm the information exists to prevent.

Standards also address a narrower population than the word suggests. Most requirements are written around wheelchair use, which is a minority of disability. Fatigue, chronic pain, sensory processing, hearing and vision loss and cognitive difference generate needs — seating along a route, predictable lighting and sound, clear signage, quiet space — that are rarely specified and cheap to provide.

The honest summary is that standards raised a floor and cannot describe a journey. What improves outcomes beyond the floor is maintenance, redundancy and accurate information, none of which appears on a completion certificate.

viewpoints.name: Commissioner Ingrid Halvorsen
viewpoints.text: We rely on individuals bringing complaints and I would change that, though not for the reason usually given. The objection is normally that it is unfair to make disabled people do the enforcing, which is true. The more decisive problem is that it produces terrible data — we learn about the venues someone had the energy to complain about, not the venues that are worst. Our map of the problem is a map of who complains. Proactive inspection would cost more and would at least tell us where we are.

viewpoints.name: Padraig Donnelly, small business owner
viewpoints.text: I run a café in a listed building and I want to comply, so this is not the objection you are expecting. I have had three different answers from three officials about what I am permitted to alter, because heritage protection and access requirements are administered separately and neither will rule on the other. I have budgeted for the work twice and cancelled twice. Give me one binding answer from one office and the ramp goes in this year. The obstacle is not the money or the will.

viewpoints.name: Dr Ayesha Rahman, legal scholar
viewpoints.text: Complaint-led enforcement is criticised as weak and the criticism is only half right. It has produced most of the significant case law, because individual cases are where standards get interpreted, and no inspection regime generates that. What it does badly is routine compliance, which is most of the problem by volume. The two mechanisms are not alternatives and are constantly discussed as though they were — you need inspection for the ordinary and litigation for the contested, and arguing about which to have is how we end up under-resourcing both.

viewpoints.name: Bram Osei, disability rights campaigner
viewpoints.text: I have brought two complaints and I would tell most people not to. The process took fourteen months, required me to document my own exclusion repeatedly, and ended in an agreement the venue then implemented slowly. I won and I would not do it again. Any enforcement model that depends on people like me is depending on a resource that runs out, and the people with the strongest case are frequently those with the least capacity to spend a year proving it.
